features.headline: Solo Ball is ahead of schedule just in time for UConn
features.desc: Solo Ball was thought to be out for the season, but his injury recovery has progressed faster than expected.
body: BOSTON — It took four months for Solo Ball to figure out what exactly was wrong with his wrist — a process that included three MRIs, five X-rays and ended with a diagnosis of multiple torn ligaments and a recovery timeline of nine months.
It only took a couple of weeks for Ball to realize he was going to beat that timeline and return to the court for UConn this season.

Just six months after surgery and three months after his wrist cast was removed, Ball could make his 2026-27 debut for the Huskies as early as Wednesday night in Las Vegas against Duke. Coach Dan Hurley said earlier this week that Ball was a game-time decision.
"Early on, it was tough, but my teammates really helped me," Ball told ESPN after UConn's win over Michigan in Boston on Nov. 6.

"The coaching staff, everyone in the locker room, everyone that's been with us this whole time in the facility, they've just been helping me a lot. And the fans gave me a lot of confidence, too. It's a whole army. That's why I love UConn."

Ball's injury, ironically, happened in his best game of the 2025-26 season. He scored 26 points and made three 3-pointers in a Dec. 16 win over Butler but hurt his wrist while bracing for a fall. Prior to the injury, Ball averaged 15.4 points.
After missing a game with the injury, Ball averaged 11.7 points over his final 27 games of the campaign that ended in the national championship game.
But given that he earned All-Big East honors in 2024-25 after posting 14.4 points and leading the league by shooting 41.4% from 3, it was clear something was wrong with Ball.

features.headline: What Aaron Rodgers' benching means for Steelers, his future
features.desc: The Steelers are starting Mason Rudolph this week over Aaron Rodgers. Why make this change now — and will it help? And is this really it for Rodgers?
body: So many of the great quarterbacks in NFL history end their careers in dramatically disappointing defeats.

Though Peyton Manning won his second Super Bowl in his final NFL start, Tom Brady went out as the quarterback of an 8-9 Buccaneers team with a 31-14 loss to the Cowboys in the wild-card playoff round. Dan Marino lost 62-7 to the Jaguars.
Drew Brees couldn't move the ball in a 30-20 playoff loss to the Vikings. Brett Favre and Steve Young were knocked out of starts by injuries and never returned.
For Aaron Rodgers, one of the greatest players in the history of the sport, the end might have come in much more mundane fashion.
In Rodgers' 267th career start, the Steelers lost 19-16 to an Eagles team with little to play for on a day when most of the headlines were devoted to ejected Steelers wideout DK Metcalf.

Two days later, the Steelers revealed in a late-night social media post that they were benching Rodgers for backup Mason Rudolph and deactivating the future Hall of Famer for Friday's game against the Broncos.
Even given the struggles the Steelers have faced on offense this season, this has to qualify as a stunning turn of events.
At 6-4, Pittsburgh is still in the thick of the playoff picture, with a 70.7% chance of advancing to the postseason per ESPN's Football Power Index. The Steelers don't appear to be rebuilding.
They appear to be suggesting that they're better off with Rudolph in the lineup than Rodgers.
There are a few questions that stand out from the story, and I want to touch on them here. There's one that I keep coming back to as I try to understand what's happening in Pittsburgh.

features.headline: Inside LeBron's first game in Philly — more than two decades ago
features.desc: Nearly 25 years ago, LeBron won over Philly for the first time — inside one of the most iconic basketball arenas in the world.
body: Jeremy Treatman, a former high school assistant coach in the Philadelphia suburbs who was running a burgeoning company that staged big-time basketball events between the game's future stars, had just sent a message to Dru Joyce II, the new coach at St. Vincent-St. Mary High School in Akron, Ohio, the school famously led by one of the most highly touted prep prospects in the history of the sport.

Six months after a then-17-year-old LeBron James had appeared on the cover of Sports Illustrated accompanied by the headline, "The Chosen One," Treatman was pitching Joyce on choosing him to build James' hype even more.

How would you like to play at the Palestra in Philly? How would you like to play Madison Square Garden against Sebastian Telfair? How would you like to play at Ohio State? How would you like to play at University of Dayton? How would you like to play in the Dean Dome in North Carolina?
In Philly parlance, Treatman had him at, "Yo."

"He calls me the next day and he says, 'You can get us to play at the Palestra?!'" Treatman told ESPN. "I go, 'Absolutely! Of course.' He goes, 'I've always dreamed of playing in the Palestra. I've heard about this place my whole life.
"I was completely bluffing about the Palestra," Treatman said. "I hadn't talked to anybody."

NAMED BY UNIVERSITY of Pennsylvania professor William N. Bates, evoking the Greek term "palæstra" that describes an athletic competition surrounded by an audience, the Palestra was the home for Penn's basketball, volleyball and wrestling teams.

features.headline: LaMelo Ball and the 'collective' carrying Minnesota without Anthony Edwards
features.desc: Through "giddiness," an enhanced focus on defense and an ensemble cast, LaMelo Ball and the Timberwolves are thriving.
body: It's Nov. 17, and the Timberwolves are hosting the Portland Trail Blazers for the second night in a row. Minnesota trails by one with 8.1 seconds remaining in the fourth quarter. The Blazers have the ball, but as Ball waits for an inbounds pass, his mind drifts to the previous possession.
With a chance to take the lead, Ball felt contact from Jrue Holiday and played it up, throwing the ball toward the basket and off the rim in an attempt to sell the foul. He didn't get the call.
"It was a bad play," Ball acknowledged later. "I knew we had to get the ball back or just make something happen."
On the next inbounds pass, he does just that.

Off the pass from Portland center Donovan Clingan, Ball beats Holiday to the ball and knocks it away. Minnesota guard Ayo Dosunmu grabs it and dashes upcourt, delivering a dart to Jaden McDaniels, who is waiting under the basket. McDaniels makes the easy layin and the Wolves take the lead, 106-105.
There are 2.6 seconds still remaining, with one of the NBA's all-time clutch players, Damian Lillard, lying in wait.

The Blazers complete the inbounds pass this time, to Lillard, who slips past McDaniels and sprints toward the basket. As Lillard floats the ball toward the rim, Trey Lyles steps in and swats it away, sealing Minnesota's improbable win.
The Wolves, at 13-5, are off to one of the best starts in franchise history.

(They started 14-4 in 2023-24.) And they've been winning mostly without star Anthony Edwards, who, after a blistering start to the 2026-27 season, has missed the past 14 games after needing right knee surgery on Oct. 29. Minnesota is 10-4 without him.

features.headline: Superlatives for this MLB free agent class, from Lowe to Gausman
features.desc: Next best move for Mets? Best free agency timing? We have a yearbook's worth of awards for the top MLB free agents.
body: We still have a week left of potential chaos before the expected lockout freezes all moves, so while we still have time, let's dig in to the MLB offseason with our annual free agent superlatives.

Not included: Tarik Skubal, the most superlative in this class. He's headed to the New York Mets, who will pay him, Juan Soto and Bo Bichette about the same as what the Milwaukee Brewers paid for their entire World Series-winning roster in 2026.
In a weak year for position players, the top two are similar-looking outfielders: Suzuki and Randy Arozarena.

Both will be entering their age-32 seasons, are coming off their best seasons (5.1 WAR for Suzuki, 5.7 for Arozarena), hit right-handed, received qualifying offers and are projected to receive four-year, $90 million contracts.

Among the teams possibly looking for a corner outfielder: the Philadelphia Phillies (25th in OPS from their corner outfielders), Baltimore Orioles (26th), Toronto Blue Jays (27th), Houston Astros (30th) and San Diego Padres (17th, but they would move Fernando Tatis Jr. to second base).
The Seattle Mariners might look to replace Arozarena with Suzuki. Which one would you rather have?

First off, given their age, both are risky bets — or, at the minimum, unlikely to repeat those 5-WAR seasons. Check out the number of position players 32 or older who had 4-or-more WAR in recent seasons (with outfielders or DHs in parenthesis):
2026: 5 (Mike Trout) 2025: 9 (Aaron Judge, George Springer, Kyle Schwarber) 2024: 4 (Judge, Marcell Ozuna) 2023: 2 2022: 5 (Springer)

features.headline: Ripple effects of Tarik Skubal signing on Mets, Dodgers and more
features.desc: The impact of the record deal for MLB's top free agent extends past his new team to the top suitors who missed out on him.
body: After finishing 20 games behind the Atlanta Braves and 14 games behind the Philadelphia Phillies in the National League East in 2026, locking up the winter's No. 1 free agent, Tarik Skubal, seemingly pushes the New York Mets closer to the teams that have largely dominated their division this decade.

That will be the case in 2027, anyway. The new collective bargaining agreement rules, whatever they are, might not go into effect until 2028 and beyond — and the Mets' long-term chances for contention could be at risk in the on-going CBA negotiations.
The ripple effects from owner Steve Cohen's $450 million investment in the two-time Cy Young Award winner will not fully take shape until after the labor agreement is concluded.
Sources on the management side report that the owners fully expect to come out of the CBA fight with a salary cap — and will pursue a hard cap on team spending.
Of course, the players will have something to say about that; the MLB Players Association leaders say they'll never agree to a cap.
If MLB's economic system changes significantly, how a contract like Skubal's might fit into the owners' vision is unknown.

The talk among some rival team officials, in the first hours after the agreement, is how much the Mets have at stake in these CBA negotiations — especially if the resulting rules don't allow owners to simply buy their way out of salary restrictions with luxury taxes.
Francisco Lindor's contract runs through 2031 at an average of $34.1 million per season, and Juan Soto's deal is for $51 million annually through 2039. Bo Bichette is set to make $42 million in 2028.
